guide.summary: This unit covers linear momentum, impulse as the time integral of force, conservation of momentum for isolated systems, elastic and inelastic collisions in one and two dimensions, explosions, and the motion of a system's center of mass.

sections.heading: Momentum and impulse
sections.body: Linear momentum p = mv is a vector. Newton's second law in its general form: ΣF = dp/dt. Impulse J = ∫F dt = Δp; the area under a force–time graph equals impulse. For the same change in momentum, a longer collision time means a smaller average force (airbags, crumple zones). An object that bounces back experiences a larger impulse than one that stops, because the change in velocity is larger.

sections.heading: Conservation of momentum
sections.body: If the net external force on a system is zero (or negligible during a brief collision), total momentum is conserved: Σp_i = Σp_f, in each direction separately. Internal forces (between objects in the system) cancel in pairs. Explosions start from rest and end with total momentum zero. The center of mass velocity v_cm = Σp/M is constant for an isolated system, even during collisions.

sections.heading: Collisions
sections.body: In all collisions, momentum is conserved. In elastic collisions, kinetic energy is also conserved; in one dimension with m₂ initially at rest: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v₁/(m₁ + m₂), v₂' = 2m₁v₁/(m₁ + m₂). Equal masses exchange velocities. In inelastic collisions, kinetic energy decreases; in perfectly inelastic collisions the objects stick together and the maximum possible kinetic energy is lost (consistent with momentum conservation). Combined problems (ballistic pendulum) use momentum conservation during the collision and energy conservation afterward. In two dimensions, conserve x- and y-momentum separately.

sections.heading: Worked example: impulse from a graph
sections.body: A force on a 2.0 kg object varies with time as a triangle peaking at 40 N at t = 0.10 s and returning to zero at t = 0.20 s. The impulse is the area under the curve: ½(0.20)(40) = 4.0 N·s, so the change in velocity is 4.0/2.0 = 2.0 m/s. Impulse equals the integral of force over time and equals the change in momentum.

sections.heading: Worked example: elastic collision
sections.body: A 1.0 kg cart moving at 6.0 m/s collides elastically with a 2.0 kg cart at rest. Using conservation of momentum and kinetic energy, the final velocities are v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = −2.0 m/s and v₂ = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 4.0 m/s. Check: momentum before = 6.0, after = −2.0 + 8.0 = 6.0 kg·m/s; kinetic energy before = 18 J, after = 2.0 + 16 = 18 J.

sections.heading: Worked example: center of mass
sections.body: For two particles, 2.0 kg at x = 0 and 6.0 kg at x = 4.0 m, the center of mass is (2.0 × 0 + 6.0 × 4.0)/8.0 = 3.0 m. For continuous objects, x_cm = (1/M)∫x dm. If no external force acts, the center of mass moves at constant velocity, even during explosions.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students forget that momentum is a vector, ignore direction signs, and assume kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions.

sections.heading: Exam connection
sections.body: Expect questions combining momentum conservation with energy, such as a ballistic pendulum, where momentum is conserved during the collision and mechanical energy afterward.

sections.heading: Laboratory and experimental design
sections.body: To test momentum conservation, collide carts on a low-friction track and record velocities with motion sensors or video before and after collisions. Compare total momentum before and after, and compare kinetic energies to classify the collision as elastic or inelastic.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body: p = mv; J = ∫F dt = Δp; Σp_i = Σp_f for isolated systems; x_cm = Σmx/Σm or (1/M)∫x dm; v_cm = Σmv/Σm.

sections.heading: Derivation tips
sections.body: When deriving collision results, write momentum conservation for each direction separately, then add energy conservation only if the collision is elastic. For explosions, total momentum is zero if the system starts at rest. Check answers by confirming that total momentum before and after matches.

sections.heading: Graph skills
sections.body: On a force-versus-time graph, the area gives impulse. On momentum-versus-time graphs for colliding objects, the total stays constant while individual momenta exchange, and the slopes are equal and opposite, showing Newton's third law during the collision.

keyTakeaways: Momentum conserved when external impulse is negligible.
Elastic: momentum and KE conserved; inelastic: only momentum.
Perfectly inelastic: objects stick; max KE loss.
Bouncing gives larger impulse than sticking.
commonMistakes: Conserving kinetic energy in inelastic collisions.
Using energy conservation during a ballistic pendulum collision.
Ignoring the vector nature of momentum (signs, components).
Thinking a stationary object can't be part of a momentum-conserving system.
examTips: Define the system and check external forces before conserving momentum.
Two-stage problems: collision (momentum), then motion (energy or kinematics).
Force–time graph questions: find area, divide by mass for Δv.
QQT FRQs: compare impulses or forces using Δp and Δt.
guide.cramSheet:
**Momentum:** p = mv · ΣF = dp/dt

**Impulse:** J = ∫F dt = Δp · area under F–t

**Conservation:** isolated → Σp_i = Σp_f (each axis)

**Elastic 1D (m₂ at rest):** v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v₁/(m₁ + m₂) · v₂' = 2m₁v₁/(m₁ + m₂)

**Perfectly inelastic:** v_f = Σp/Σm

**COM:** v_cm = Σp/M constant if isolated

vocab.definition: The product of mass and velocity, p = mv.
The integral of force over time, equal to the change in momentum.
A system with no net external force.
The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant.
A collision in which total kinetic energy is conserved.
A collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved.
A collision in which objects stick together.
An event where internal forces push parts of a system apart; total momentum is unchanged.
A device that uses a perfectly inelastic collision followed by a swing to measure a projectile's speed.
Total momentum divided by total mass.
Impulse divided by the collision time.
The ratio of relative speeds after and before a collision (1 for elastic).

practice.stem: A force F(t) = 6t² (N) acts on an object from t = 0 to t = 2 s. What impulse does it deliver?

choices.text: A stops and B moves at 3 m/s

practice.explanation: Equal masses exchange velocities in a 1D elastic collision.

practice.stem: Why does an airbag reduce injury in a crash?

choices.text: It reduces the change in momentum of the occupant.
It increases the time over which the occupant stops, reducing the average force.

practice.explanation: Same Δp over a longer Δt means smaller force.

practice.stem: A 2.0 kg ball moving at 6.0 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 4.0 kg ball at rest. What are their velocities afterward?
In the collision where a 2.0 kg cart at 6.0 m/s sticks to a 4.0 kg cart at rest, how much kinetic energy is lost?
practice.explanation: Initial K = 36 J; final K = ½(6)(2²) = 12 J; lost 24 J.

practice.stem: A 10 g bullet moving at 400 m/s embeds in a 2.0 kg block hanging from a string. How high does the block swing? (g = 9.8 m/s²)

distractors.D: Uses energy conservation through the collision.

practice.stem: Two carts collide on a frictionless track. Which quantity is the same before and after the collision regardless of collision type?

choices.text: Velocity of the center of mass

practice.explanation: v_cm = p_total/M, and p_total is conserved.

practice.stem: A 1.0 kg puck moving east at 4.0 m/s strikes a 1.0 kg puck at rest on frictionless ice. Afterward, the first puck moves at 2.0 m/s at 60° north of east. What is the speed of the second puck? (cos 60° = 0.50, sin 60° ≈ 0.87)
In the puck collision above, is the collision elastic?
practice.stimulus: Before: 1.0 kg at 4.0 m/s east; 1.0 kg at rest. After: first puck 2.0 m/s at 60° north of east; second puck about 3.5 m/s at 30° south of east.

choices.text: Yes: total kinetic energy is 8.0 J before and after, and the pucks move off at 90° to each other.
No: kinetic energy decreases by half.
It cannot be determined without the collision time.

practice.explanation: Before: ½(1)(16) = 8.0 J. After: ½(1)(4) + ½(1)(12) = 8.0 J. For equal masses with one initially at rest, an elastic glancing collision always sends them off at right angles.

practice.stem: A 60 kg person stands at one end of a 20 kg, 4.0 m boat at rest on still water and walks to the other end. Ignoring water resistance, how far does the boat move?
practice.explanation: COM stays fixed: 60(4 − d) = 20d → 240 = 80d → d = 3.0 m.

practice.stem: A net force on a 2.0 kg object varies as F(t) = 8 − 2t (N) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 s. If the object starts at rest, what is its maximum speed during this interval?
practice.explanation: F stays positive until t = 4, so speed increases throughout. J = ∫(8 − 2t) dt from 0 to 4 = 32 − 16 = 16 N·s; v = 16/2 = 8 m/s.

practice.prompt: Two balls of equal mass m are thrown horizontally at the same speed v toward a heavy block resting on a frictionless floor. Ball 1 is made of clay and sticks to the block. Ball 2 is rubber and bounces straight back with speed v (elastic). The block's mass M is much greater than m.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that the clay ball gives the block a larger speed because it 'stays with' the block. Without equations, explain which ball gives the block a larger speed.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive expressions for the impulse each ball exerts on the block in terms of m and v, treating the block as nearly stationary during the collision.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain how your expressions support or contradict your answer to (A).

rubric.description: The rubber ball gives the block a larger speed.
The rubber ball's momentum reverses, so its change in momentum is larger than the clay ball's, which only stops.
By Newton's third law / momentum conservation, the block gains momentum equal to the ball's loss, so it gains more from the rubber ball.
Δp_ball = 0 − mv → impulse on block ≈ mv.
Uses J = Δp and Newton's third law (impulse on block equals negative impulse on ball).
2mv > mv: the rubber ball delivers twice the impulse.
Block's speed ∝ impulse/M, so it is larger for the rubber ball, consistent with (A).

practice.sampleResponse:
A. The rubber ball gives the block a larger speed. The clay ball's momentum only goes to zero, but the rubber ball's momentum reverses direction, so its momentum changes by a greater amount. Because the ball and block exert equal and opposite forces on each other during the same contact time, the block's momentum changes by an equal and opposite amount, so the block gains more momentum from the rubber ball.

B. Impulse on a ball equals its change in momentum, and by Newton's third law the impulse on the block is equal and opposite. Clay ball: Δp = 0 − mv = −mv, so the block receives an impulse of mv. Rubber ball: Δp = (−mv) − (mv) = −2mv, so the block receives an impulse of 2mv.

C. The rubber ball delivers an impulse of 2mv, twice the clay ball's mv. Since the block's final speed is its impulse divided by its mass, the rubber ball gives the block about twice the speed, supporting my answer to (A) and contradicting the student's claim.
